readings.c2s1:
¶
'''thow'''<sup>3</sup>, ''v.'' and ''n.'' A dialectal variant of ''thaw.''

'''thowel, thowl,''' ''n.'' Variants of ''thole''<sup>2</sup>.

'''thowless''' (thou′les), ''a.'' [A var. of ''thewless.'' Cf. ''thieveless.''] Slack; inactive; lazy. [Scotch.]

{{smaller block|I will not wait upon the ''thowless'', thriftless, fissenless ministry of that carnal man, John Halftext, the curate.
{{right|''Scott'', Old Mortality, v.}}}}

'''thowmbe†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''thumb''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Thracian''' (thrā′shan), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< L. ''Thracius'', Thracian, ''Thracia'', Thrace, < Gr. Θρᾴκιος, Ionic Θρηΐκιος, Θρήκιος, Thracian, < Θρᾴκη, Ionic Θρῄκη, Thrace, < Θρᾷξ, Ionic Θρήϊξ, Θρῇξ, a Thracian.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to Thrace, a region in southeastern Europe (formerly a Roman province), included between the Balkans and the Ægean and Black Seas.

{{smaller block|The riot of the tipsy Bacchanals,
Tearing the ''Thracian'' singer in their rage.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., v. 1. 49.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' An inhabitant or a native of Thrace.

'''thrack†''' (thrak), ''v. t.'' [Appar. < ME. *''threkken'', ''thrucchen'', < AS. ''thryccan'' (= OHG. ''drucchen'', MHG. ''drucken'', ''drücken'', G. ''drücken'', etc.), press, oppress.] To load or burden.

{{smaller block|Certainly we shall one day find that the strait gate is too narrow for any man to come bustling in, ''thrack'd'' with great possessions and greater corruptions.
{{right|''South'', Sermons, II. vi.}}}}

'''thragge†''', ''v. t.'' Apparently an error for ''shragge'' (see ''shrag'').

{{smaller block|Fell, or cutte downe, or to ''thragge.'' Succido.
{{right|''Huloet'', Abecedarium (1552). (''Nares.'')}}}}

'''thral†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''thrall.''

'''thraldom''' (thrâl′dum), ''n.'' [Also ''thralldom'', and formerly ''thraldome''; < ME. ''thraldom'' (= Icel. ''thrældōmr'' = Sw. ''träldom'' = Dan. ''trældom''); < ''thrall'' + ''-dom.''] The state or character of being a thrall; bondage, literal or figurative; servitude.

{{smaller block|Every base affection
Keeps him [man] in slavish ''t[h]raldome'' & subjection.
{{right|''Times' Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 93.}}}}

{{smaller block|“Such as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God,” and not such as live in ''thraldom'' unto men.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, iii. 9.}}}}

'''thralhood†''' (thrâl′hu̇d), ''n.'' [ME. ''thralhod, thralhede''; < ''thrall'' + ''-hood.''] Thraldom.

{{smaller block|Thanne is mi ''thralhod'',
Iwent in to kniȝthod.
{{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 13.}}}}

'''thrall''' (thrâl), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< ME. ''thral, thralle, threl, threlle'' (pl. ''thralles, thrales, threlles, threles''), < late AS. ''thrǣl'' (pl. ''thrǣlas''), < Icel. ''thræll'' = Sw. ''träl'' = Dan. ''træl'', a thrall, prob. = OHG. ''dregil, drigil, trigil, trikil'', a serf, thrall; Teut. form *''thragila'' (contracted in Scand.), perhaps orig. ‘a runner,’ hence an attendant, servant; < AS. ''thrægian'' (= Goth. ''thragjan''), run, < ''thrag, thrah'', a running, course; cf. Gr. τροχίλος, a small bird said to be attendant on the crocodile, < τρόχος, a running, < τρέχειν, run (see ''trochil, trochus'', etc.). {{RunningHeader|thoughtful|6304|thrall}}{{smaller block|And oh! what business had she to be so ungrateful and to try and thwart Philip in his ''thoughtful'' wish of escorting them through the streets of the rough, riotous town? {{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Sylvia's Lovers, iii.}}}} 5. Full of care; anxious; troubled. {{smaller block|O ''thoughtful'' herte, plungyd in dystres. {{right|''Lydgate'', Life of Our Lady. (''Hoppe''.)}}}} {{smaller block|Around her crowd distrust and doubt and fear, And ''thoughtful'' foresight and tormenting care. {{right|''Prior''.}}}} {{smaller|=Syn. 1. Reflective, pensive, studious.—3. Considerate, regardful.}} '''thoughtfully''' (thât′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In a thoughtful or considerate manner; with thought or solicitude. '''thoughtfulness''' (thât′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The state of being thoughtful; meditation; serious attention; considerateness; solicitude. '''thoughtless''' (thât′les), ''a.'' [< ''thought''1 + ''-less''.] 1. Devoid of or lacking capacity for thought. {{smaller block|Just as a blockhead rubs his ''thoughtless'' skull, And thanks his stars he was not born a fool. {{right|''Pope'', Epil. to Rowe's Jane Shore, l. 7.}}}} {{smaller block|A fair average human skull, which might have belonged to a philosopher, or might have contained the ''thoughtless'' brains of a savage. ''Huxley'', Man's Place in Nature, p. 181.}} 2. Unthinking; heedless; careless; giddy. {{smaller block|He was lively, witty, good-natur'd, and a pleasant companion, but idle, ''thoughtless'', and imprudent to the last degree. {{right|''Franklin'', Autobiog., p. 159.}}}} {{smaller block|They cajole with gold And promises of fame the ''thoughtless'' youth. {{right|''Shelley'', Queen Mab, iv.}}}} {{smaller block|That ''thoughtless'' sense of joy bewildering That kisses youthful hearts amidst of spring.}} with others of wolves. {{smaller|The group is not well marked, but has been made to cover several African forms which represent the peculiar South American fox-wolves, and come under the general head of jackals. Some of them are brindled with light and dark colors on the back. Among them are ''T. anthus'', the wild dog of Egypt; ''T. variegatus'', the Nubian thous; ''T. mesomelas'', the black-backed or Cape jackal; ''T. senegalensis'', the Senegal thous or jackal; etc. See also cut under ''jackal''.}} 2. [''l. c.''] A jackal of this genus: as, the Senegal ''thous''. '''thousand''' (thou′zand), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''thousand'', ''thousend'', ''thusend'', < AS. ''thūsend'' = OS. ''thusund-ig'' = OFries. ''thūsend'', ''dūsent'' = D. ''duizend'' = OLG. ''thūsint'', MLG. ''dusent'', LG. ''dusend'' = OHG. ''thūsunt'', ''dūsunt'', ''tūsent'', MHG. ''tūsent'', ''tūsunt'', G. ''tausend'' = Icel. ''thūsund'' (also ''thūshund'', ''thūshundradh'', conformed to ''hund'', ''hundradh'', hundred) = Sw. ''tusen'' = Dan. ''tusende'' = Goth. ''thūsundi'', thousand. Though all numerals up to 100 belong in common to all the Indo-Eur. languages, this word for ''thousand'' is found only in the Teut. and Slav. languages: = OBulg. ''tysanshta'' = Serv. ''tisuca'' = Pol. ''tysiac'' = Russ. ''tysiacha'' = OPruss. ''tūsimtons'' (pl. acc.) = Lith. ''tukstantis'' = Lett. ''tūkstōts'', etc. Possibly the Slavs borrowed the word in prehistoric times from the Teut.] I. ''a.'' Numbering ten hundred; hence, of an indefinitely large number. {{smaller block|Themperour hire throli thonked many ''thousand'' sithe. {{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 5154.}}}} {{smaller block|That Cry Which made me look a ''thousand'' ways In bush, and tree, and sky. {{right|''Wordsworth'', To the Cuckoo. ''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 396.}}}} {{smaller block|=Syn. 2. ''Heedless, Remiss,'' etc. (see ''negligent''), regardless, inattentive, inconsiderate, unmindful, flighty, harebrained.}} '''thoughtlessly''' (thât′les-li), ''adv.'' In a thoughtless, inconsiderate, or careless manner; without thought. {{smaller block|In restless hurries ''thoughtlessly'' they live. {{right|''Garth.''}}}} '''thoughtlessness''' (thât′les-nes), ''n.'' The state of being thoughtless, heedless, or inconsiderate. {{smaller block|What is called absence is a ''thoughtlessness'' and want of attention about what is doing. {{right|''Chesterfield.''}}}} '''thought-reader''' (thât′rē″dėr), ''n.'' A mind-reader. {{smaller block|We are all convinced that when mistakes are made the fault rests, for the most part, with the thinkers, rather than with the ''thought-readers.'' {{right|''Proc. Soc. Psych. Research'', I. 43.}}}} '''thoughtsick''' (thât′sik), ''a.'' [< ''thought'' + ''sick.''] Sick from thinking. {{smaller block|Heaven's face doth glow; Yea, this solidity and compound mass, With tristful visage, as against the doom, Is ''thought-sick'' at the act. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 4. 51.}}}} '''thoughtsome''' (thât′sum), ''a.'' [< ''thought''1 + ''-some.''] Thoughtful. ''Encyc. Dict.'' '''II.''' ''n.'' 1. The number ten hundred, or ten times ten times ten; hence, indefinitely, a great number. {{smaller|Like ''hundred, million,'' etc., ''thousand'' takes a plural termination when not preceded by a numeral adjective.}} {{smaller block|Ther com . . . xlMI [people], what on horse bakke and on fote, with-oute hem that were in the town, whereof ther were vjMI; but the story seith that in tho dayes fyve hundred was cleped a ''thousande.'' {{right|''Merlin'' (E.
